memorize.back: b̂_1 = Cov(X, Y) / Var(X) = Σ(X_i − X̄)(Y_i − Ȳ) / Σ(X_i − X̄)²
e_i = Y_i − Ŷ_i = Y_i − (b̂_0 + b̂_1 X_i)

memorize.front: Four assumptions of simple linear regression
memorize.back: Linearity; homoskedasticity (constant error variance); independence of errors; normally distributed errors

memorize.front: BA II Plus LIN output names
memorize.back: a = intercept b̂_0; b = slope b̂_1; r = correlation

traps: Swapping X and Y when entering data
Reading the BA II Plus 'a' as the slope (it is the intercept)
Interpreting the intercept far outside the range of the data

story_idea.candidate: In 1886 Francis Galton published 'Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature', based on the heights of 928 adult children of 205 pairs of parents in England. Children of very tall parents were tall, but on average less extreme than their parents.
story_idea.why: Why do the children of exceptionally tall parents tend to be less exceptional — and how do you draw the one 'best' line through a cloud of points?

days.module: LM10 Applications of Simple Linear Regression in Finance
days.title: ANOVA, R² and the standard error
days.concept: Total variation in Y splits into an explained part and an unexplained part, SST = SSR + SSE; R² = SSR/SST measures the fit, the standard error of estimate √(SSE/(n − 2)) measures the typical miss, and F = MSR/MSE tests whether the slope explains anything at all.
los: SST = Σ(Y_i − Ȳ)² = SSR + SSE
R² = SSR/SST = r² in simple regression
MSR = SSR/1; MSE = SSE/(n − 2)
F = MSR/MSE with (1, n − 2) df
Standard error of estimate SEE = √MSE
A high R² is not causation; Anscombe-type data need plots

calculator.task: An ANOVA table with n = 30, SSR = 0.0040 and SSE = 0.0060: R², MSE, SEE and the F-statistic with its p-value; then r² from the Day 47 LIN data
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic; LIN r then x² for R²; F critical value from a table
calculator.ti: Home screen; LinReg(a+bx) with DiagnosticOn shows r²; Fcdf( for the p-value

memorize.back: SST = SSR + SSE
R² = SSR / SST (= r² with one independent variable)
MSE = SSE / (n − 2)
SEE = √MSE = √[SSE / (n − 2)]
F = MSR / MSE = (SSR / 1) / [SSE / (n − 2)], df = 1 and n − 2

traps: Dividing SSE by n − 1 instead of n − 2
Confusing the SEE with the standard error of the slope
Reading a high R² as proof of causation or of a good model

story_idea.candidate: In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe published four small datasets — now 'Anscombe's quartet' — with the same means, variances, correlation (about 0.816) and fitted line (Y = 3 + 0.5X), yet wildly different shapes when plotted.
story_idea.why: If four datasets have the same R² and the same line, does the regression fit all four equally well — and what does R² actually measure?

days.module: LM10 Applications of Simple Linear Regression in Finance
days.title: Testing the slope; beta by regression
days.concept: The slope's t-statistic, (b̂_1 − B_1)/s_b̂1 with n − 2 df, tests whether X really moves Y; regressing a stock's returns on the market's gives its beta, and in simple regression the slope test is the same as the correlation test t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²).

CAPM beta by regression: Y = stock excess (or total) returns, X = market returns; intercept = alpha
Test of the intercept

story_idea.candidate: In June 1992 Eugene Fama and Kenneth French published 'The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns' in the Journal of Finance, finding that from 1963 to 1990 a stock's beta did little to explain its average return once size and book-to-market were considered — headlines declared 'beta is dead'.
story_idea.why: A fitted slope is never exactly zero. How do you decide whether beta really explains returns or the slope is just noise?

days.module: LM10 Applications of Simple Linear Regression in Finance
days.title: Forecasts, prediction intervals and log models
days.concept: A regression forecast Ŷ_f = b̂_0 + b̂_1X_f comes with a prediction interval Ŷ_f ± t_c × s_f that widens as X_f moves away from X̄, and taking logs of Y and/or X lets a straight line fit exponential growth or elasticities.

s_f² = SEE² × [1 + 1/n + (X_f − X̄)²/((n − 1)s_X²)]
Prediction interval Ŷ_f ± t_c s_f, df = n − 2
Log-lin ln Y = b_0 + b_1X (b_1 ≈ continuous growth rate per unit of X); lin-log Y = b_0 + b_1 ln X; log-log ln Y = b_0 + b_1 ln X (b_1 = elasticity)

memorize.back: s_f² = SEE² × [1 + 1/n + (X_f − X̄)² / ((n − 1) s_X²)]
Ŷ_f ± t_c × s_f, df = n − 2
ln Y = b_0 + b_1 X; forecast Y = e^(b_0 + b_1 X)
b_1 = elasticity: % change in Y for a 1% change in X

traps: Using the SEE alone as the forecast's standard error
Forgetting to exponentiate a log-lin forecast back to Y
Ignoring that the interval widens as X_f moves away from X̄

story_idea.candidate: In the 19 April 1965 issue of Electronics, Gordon Moore (later a co-founder of Intel) predicted in 'Cramming more components onto integrated circuits' that the number of components on a chip would keep doubling about every year; in 1975 he revised it to about every two years.
story_idea.why: Growth that doubles on schedule is a curve, not a line. How can a straight-line regression measure it — and how sure can a forecast ten years out be?

days.module: Portfolio Risk and Return: Part II
days.title: Beta, CAPM and the security market line
days.concept: Only systematic risk is rewarded, so an asset's expected return is E(R_i) = R_f + β_i[E(R_m) − R_f] with β_i = Cov(R_i, R_m)/σ_m² = ρ_im σ_i/σ_m; an asset that plots above the security market line is undervalued (positive alpha).
los: β_i = Cov(R_i, R_m)/σ_m² = ρ_im σ_i/σ_m
CAPM: E(R_i) = R_f + β_i[E(R_m) − R_f] (cost of equity, Equities)
Security market line (β on the x-axis) vs capital market line (σ on the x-axis)
Alpha = forecast return − CAPM required return; above SML → undervalued
Systematic vs unsystematic risk; market model R_i = α_i + β_iR_m + e_i
Multi-factor/APT: E(R) = R_f + Σ β_k λ_k (explain)

calculator.task: ρ = 0.6, σ_i = 30%, σ_m = 18%: beta; then CAPM with R_f = 4% and an equity risk premium of 5.5%; an analyst forecasts 14% — alpha and the verdict
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: β_i = Cov(R_i, R_m) / σ_m² = ρ_im × σ_i / σ_m
E(R_i) = R_f + β_i × [E(R_m) − R_f]
α = forecast (or actual) return − CAPM required return; α > 0 → undervalued
E(R_p) = R_F + λ_1 β_p,1 + … + λ_K β_p,K
CML: total risk σ (efficient portfolios); SML: beta (any asset or portfolio)

traps: Multiplying beta by the market return instead of the market risk premium
Using σ (CML) to price an individual stock
Calling a stock above the SML overvalued

story_idea.candidate: On Monday 8 August 2011, the first trading day after Standard & Poor's cut the United States' credit rating from AAA to AA+, the S&P 500 fell about 6.7% while gold rose to a record above $1,700 an ounce; gold went on to peak near $1,900 in early September 2011. Over long periods gold's price swings have been roughly as large as stocks', yet it has earned far less.
story_idea.why: If gold is about as volatile as stocks, why do investors accept a much lower long-run return for holding it — which kind of risk does the market actually pay for?

days.module: Portfolio Risk and Return: Part II
days.title: Risk-adjusted performance measures
days.concept: Risk-adjusted measures compare excess return with the risk that matters: the Sharpe ratio uses total risk σ, Treynor and Jensen's alpha use beta, M² restates the Sharpe ratio as a return at the market's risk, and Sortino and Calmar look at downside risk and drawdowns.
los: Sharpe = (R_p − R_f)/σ_p
Treynor = (R_p − R_f)/β_p
M² = (R_p − R_f) × σ_m/σ_p − (R_m − R_f)
Jensen's alpha α_p = R_p − [R_f + β_p(R_m − R_f)]
Sortino = (R_p − MAR)/downside deviation; Calmar = annualized return/maximum drawdown (Alternatives)
Which measure for which portfolio (diversified vs not)

calculator.task: A fund returns 12% with σ = 4% and β = 0.3; the market returns 10% with σ = 15%; R_f = 3%: Sharpe, Treynor, M² and Jensen's alpha for fund and market
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: Sharpe = (R_p − R_f) / σ_p
Treynor = (R_p − R_f) / β_p
M² = (R_p − R_f) × (σ_m / σ_p) − (R_m − R_f); equivalently, the risk-adjusted return R_f + (R_p − R_f) × σ_m/σ_p compared with R_m
α_p = R_p − [R_f + β_p (R_m − R_f)]
Sortino = (R_p − MAR) / downside deviation

traps: Using Treynor or Jensen for a portfolio that is not well diversified
Forgetting to subtract (R_m − R_f) in M²
Ranking by raw return instead of risk-adjusted return

story_idea.candidate: In a November 2005 memo to the SEC titled 'The World's Largest Hedge Fund is a Fraud', the analyst Harry Markopolos argued that Bernard Madoff's steady returns of about 1% a month, with almost no losing months, were mathematically implausible. Madoff was arrested on 11 December 2008.
story_idea.why: How can returns be too good — and what single number would have flagged Madoff's record as suspicious?

days.module: Curve-Based and Empirical Fixed-Income Risk Measures
days.title: Effective duration and negative convexity
days.concept: When cash flows change with interest rates — callable bonds and mortgage securities — sensitivity must be measured by repricing under shifts of the benchmark curve, EffDur = (PV_− − PV_+)/(2 × ΔCurve × PV_0), and prepayments give mortgage securities negative convexity.

Effective convexity EffCon = [(PV_−) + (PV_+) − 2PV_0]/[(ΔCurve)² × PV_0]
Negative convexity of callable bonds and MBS
Key rate durations: sensitivity to one maturity's rate; they sum to effective duration
Mortgage prepayment: SMM and CPR = 1 − (1 − SMM)^12; PSA benchmark, WAM, WAC, WAL, LTV (describe)

EffCon = [PV_− + PV_+ − 2 × PV_0] / [(ΔCurve)² × PV_0]

story_idea.candidate: In early 1994, after the Federal Reserve began raising rates on 4 February, David Askin's Granite funds — about $600 million invested in complex mortgage-backed securities marketed as market-neutral — collapsed within weeks as prepayments slowed and prices fell faster than his models predicted.
story_idea.why: Why can a mortgage bond lose more when rates rise than it gains when rates fall, and why does ordinary duration miss it?

days.module: Credit Risk
days.title: Credit risk: expected loss and spreads
days.concept: Expected loss equals the probability of default times the loss given default (exposure × (1 − recovery rate)); the credit spread is roughly that annual expected loss, and a spread change moves a bond's price by about −ModDur × ΔSpread + ½ × Convexity × (ΔSpread)².

Yield spread ≈ POD × LGD (per year)
Price impact of a spread change: %ΔPV ≈ −ModDur × ΔSpread + ½ × Convexity × (ΔSpread)²
Credit ratios: EBITDA/interest, debt/EBITDA, FFO/debt, debt/capital (higher leverage → weaker credit)
Seniority ranking and recovery; credit migration

calculator.task: A recovery of 8.625 per 100: the LGD; a 3% annual default probability gives an expected loss and approximate spread; a bond with ModDur 6.5 and convexity 55 when its spread widens 300 bp
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with x²

memorize.back: EL = probability of default × loss given default
LGD = exposure × (1 − recovery rate)
Spread ≈ POD × LGD (as % of exposure per year)

memorize.back: %ΔPV ≈ −ModDur × ΔSpread + ½ × Convexity × (ΔSpread)²

memorize.front: Leverage ratios used by credit analysts
memorize.back: Debt/EBITDA, FFO/debt, debt/capital; coverage: EBITDA/interest

story_idea.why: How can a company report billions of profit to shareholders and almost none to the tax authority — and where on its balance sheet does the difference show up?

A rate cut lowers a net DTA (raises tax expense) and lowers a net DTL (cuts tax expense)

days.module: Analyzing Income Statements
days.title: Basic and diluted EPS
days.concept: Basic EPS divides earnings available to common shareholders by the weighted-average shares outstanding; diluted EPS adds the extra shares that convertibles, options and warrants would create — and adds back what they cost — using the if-converted and treasury stock methods, and ignores anything antidilutive.

Weighted-average shares; stock splits and stock dividends applied retroactively
If-converted method: convertible preferred (add back preferred dividends) and convertible bonds (add back interest × (1 − t))

Equities link: effects of share repurchases and splits on shares and EPS

days.module: Analyzing Statements of Cash Flows I
days.title: Cash from operations: indirect and direct
days.concept: Profit and cash differ: the indirect method starts with net income, adds back non-cash charges and losses, subtracts gains, and adjusts for working capital (an increase in an operating asset uses cash, an increase in an operating liability provides it), while the direct method rebuilds cash received and paid line by line.

Direct method: cash from customers = revenue − ΔAR; cash paid to suppliers = COGS + ΔInventory − ΔAP; cash paid for other items
Converting indirect to direct
Classification: interest and dividends paid/received under IFRS vs US GAAP
CFI and CFF items

story_idea.why: How can a company report a profit year after year and still run out of cash?

days.module: Analyzing Statements of Cash Flows II

Payables turnover = purchases/average payables; DPO = 365/payables turnover

days.module: Equity Valuation: Concepts and Basic Tools

story_idea.candidate: On 25 April 2019 the UK Competition and Markets Authority blocked the £7.3 billion merger of Sainsbury's and Asda, Britain's second- and third-largest supermarket chains, concluding that the combined group would hold close to 30% of the grocery market and that prices would rise.
story_idea.why: Two supermarkets merging leaves plenty of rivals. How do regulators put a single number on how concentrated a market is — and on how much one merger changes it?

days.module: Alternative Investment Performance and Returns
days.title: Hedge-fund fees: from gross to net
days.concept: Hedge-fund investors earn the gross return minus a management fee and an incentive fee on profits above any hurdle and high-water mark, so a '2 and 20' fund must earn a large gross return just to match an index fund, and a fund of funds adds a second layer of fees.
los: Management fee on assets (beginning or ending NAV, or committed capital)
Incentive fee: on gross gains or net of the management fee; hard hurdle (fee on gains above the hurdle) vs soft hurdle (fee on all gains once the hurdle is cleared)
High-water mark: no incentive fee until previous peak NAV is regained
Fund-of-funds double fees
Gross vs net return; NAV per share = (assets − liabilities)/shares outstanding
Leveraged return R_L = R + (V_B/V_E)(R − r_D) (2027 coverage uncertain — insurance)

calculator.task: A fund grows from $100 million to $120 million; 2% management fee on ending assets, 20% incentive fee net of the management fee above a 5% hard hurdle: the fees and the investor's net return; then year 2 with a high-water mark after a loss
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: Net return = (ending NAV after all fees − beginning NAV) / beginning NAV

memorize.front: Incentive fee net of management fee, hard hurdle
memorize.back: Incentive = rate × max[0, ending assets − management fee − beginning assets × (1 + hurdle)]
Incentive fees are paid only on value above the highest previous NAV (net of fees)
R_L = R + (V_B / V_E) × (R − r_D)

traps: Charging the incentive fee on gross gains when the terms say net of the management fee
Ignoring the high-water mark after a losing year
Treating a soft hurdle like a hard hurdle

story_idea.candidate: In 2007 Warren Buffett bet Ted Seides of Protégé Partners $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a hand-picked group of five funds of hedge funds over the ten years 2008-2017. The index fund returned about 7.1% a year; the funds of funds averaged about 2.2%. Girls Inc. of Omaha received the winnings.
story_idea.why: Hedge-fund managers are often skilled. How can fees alone turn decent gross returns into poor net returns, and how big a gross return does '2 and 20' (plus another layer) require?

days.module: Alternative Investment Performance and Returns
days.title: Private equity waterfalls, IRR and MOIC
days.concept: In private equity the distribution waterfall decides when the general partner earns carried interest — after investors have their capital and preferred return back, either across the whole fund (European) or deal by deal (American), with catch-up and clawback provisions — and performance is reported as IRR and the multiple of invested capital.
los: European (whole-of-fund) vs American (deal-by-deal) waterfall
Preferred return (hurdle), full catch-up, carried interest
Clawback of excess carry paid early
MOIC = (realized value + unrealized value)/invested capital
IRR of the fund's cash flows (CF worksheet); IRR vs MOIC (time ignored)

calculator.task: A fund's cash flows to investors of −100, −50, +40, +90, +120 (years 0-4): the IRR and MOIC; then the GP's carry under a European waterfall with an 8% preferred return, full catch-up and 20% carry
calculator.ba: CF worksheet IRR CPT; chain arithmetic for the waterfall

memorize.back: MOIC = (realized value + unrealized value) / total invested capital
LPs receive all contributed capital plus the preferred return before the GP earns carry
Carry is paid on each deal as it is exited (earlier for the GP; clawback risk for LPs)
After the preferred return, the GP receives (most or all of) distributions until it has its full carry share of total profits
GP must return carry received in excess of its entitled share over the life of the fund

traps: Thinking the American waterfall is more favourable to LPs
Comparing funds by MOIC alone (it ignores time)
Forgetting the catch-up when computing the GP's carry

story_idea.candidate: When Blackstone filed to go public in 2007, its prospectus revealed that co-founder Stephen Schwarzman had received about $398 million for 2006, much of it from carried interest on the firm's buyout funds.
story_idea.why: A private-equity manager's fee is supposedly '2 and 20'. How does a fund's profit actually flow between investors and managers, so that one manager can earn hundreds of millions in a year?
